metadata.title: A Polished Output Is Not Evidence the Work Is Correct.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: does a polished, confident answer mean the work underneath is correct? Lands the carry-out that fluency and accuracy come from different things — only checking the source tells them apart.
metadata.anchor_pair: B03 -> B08 (the three-citation summary: planted as a clean-reading document that only opening each source catches; returned run through the source checks and logged as the reel closes)
metadata.one_flag: B06 - if the agent actually used a tool to open the file, that check is real; you can't tell which case you're in from the fluent report alone

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes a polished, confident answer from Claude must be correct. It isn't — confidence there just means the writing is fluent. So what actually tells you the work is right?

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'A polished, confident answer from Claude means it's correct — right?', hesitates on 'correct', corrects to 'fluent'

props.text:
A polished, confident
answer from Claude
means it's correct —
right?

beats.note: B00 is Remotion (BrutalistHesitantWriter) per hai-simple SKILL.md WRITER LAW. TIMING LAW: narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('correct' -> 'fluent') is visible on a late frame.

beats.narration_text: Claude can hand back a citation, a claim, and a number in the same fluent paragraph, in exactly the same confident voice. Nothing in how it reads tells you which parts were checked and which were invented.

shot.new_visual_element: a citation card, a claim card, a number card, all carrying the same confident 'voice' mark

production_viz.label: Same confident voice, three outputs
production_viz.mechanic: Three small pill cards in a row: CITATION, CLAIM, NUMBER. Each glows with an identical small 'confident voice' mark above it. Caption beneath: 'checked or invented — same voice'.

beats.narration_text: So the natural read: if the writing is this polished and organized, the sourcing underneath is probably solid too. Confidence feels like it has to be earned.

shot.new_visual_element: a polished passage, a checkmark forming underneath it

production_viz.label: The natural guess
production_viz.mechanic: A block of neatly organized text with headings. A confident checkmark forms beneath it, captioned 'polished = solid sourcing?'.

beats.narration_text: Here's the case that breaks it. A summary came back with precise phrasing and three careful citations — polished enough that she opened all three. One paper didn't exist. One said the opposite of what the summary claimed. One was from an unrelated field entirely.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR - three citation cards, each snapping from confident TEAL to broken CRIMSON in sequence

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR - three citations, three breaks
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Three citation cards in a row, each formatted cleanly, each glowing TEAL. In sequence, each snaps to CRIMSON as its failure is revealed underneath: 'DOES NOT EXIST', 'SAYS OPPOSITE', 'WRONG FIELD'. THESE EXACT THREE CARDS RETURN AT B08.

beats.narration_text: Language models are trained to produce fluent, coherent, well organized text. That training target is coherence, not accuracy — so the model gets very good at one thing: sounding right.

shot.new_visual_element: two bars, FLUENCY (trained, tall, TEAL) and ACCURACY (not the target, CRIMSON question mark)

production_viz.label: What training actually targets
production_viz.mechanic: Two vertical bars side by side: FLUENCY, tall and fully filled TEAL; ACCURACY, shorter, CRIMSON, topped with a question mark. A label 'training target' points only to FLUENCY.

beats.narration_text: High-confidence prose is structurally uncorrelated with correctness. The accurate paragraph and the invented one come from the exact same process — you cannot tell them apart just by reading.

shot.new_visual_element: two identical-looking paragraphs, one quietly labeled TRUE, one FABRICATED

production_viz.label: Identical on the surface
production_viz.mechanic: Two paragraph blocks, visually identical in formatting and tone. Small labels fade in beneath each — one 'TRUE', one 'FABRICATED' — the only difference, and it's invisible from the text itself.

beats.narration_text: This means the agent's own report isn't evidence either. 'I checked the sources' can mean it matched citation text against memory, never opening a document. One flag: if the agent actually used a tool to open the file, that check is real — but you can't tell which case you're in from the fluent report alone.

shot.new_visual_element: THE FLAG - a clipboard reading 'checked' beside a locked source document, a single terracotta flag marker

production_viz.label: THE ONE FLAG - a report is not a check
production_viz.mechanic: A single terracotta FLAG marker over the beat, the reel's only hedge, labeled as one. A clipboard reads 'CHECKED' beside a source document shown behind a lock icon, with a dashed line between them (no real connection shown). Caption: 'unless a tool actually opened it'.

beats.narration_text: Carlos asks an agent to draft a policy brief citing five government reports in a folder. It reads two — three are password protected — and fills the rest from training data, producing plausible-looking citations to all five. Carlos spot-checks one claim: the cited page says the opposite.

shot.new_visual_element: five report icons, two filled TEAL ('read'), three CRIMSON ('locked'); one citation marked wrong

production_viz.label: Carlos: 5 cited, 2 read, 1 caught wrong
production_viz.mechanic: Five report icons in a row: two fill TEAL ('read'), three stay CRIMSON ('locked'). Below, a brief document shows five citations; one gets a CRIMSON mark reading 'says opposite' when Carlos spot-checks it.

beats.narration_text: Run the original summary back through: open each source — one confirmed nonexistent, one confirmed contradicting, one confirmed off-topic. That's a record now, not a guess. But checking three claims doesn't make the rest of the document airtight — it only covers what got opened. And one bad citation doesn't mean the whole report is worthless — it means that one claim needs redoing.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - the three cards, now logged as confirmed broken; two dimmed captions beneath

production_viz.label: The record, then both directions
production_viz.mechanic: THE B03 ANCHOR RETURNS: the same three citation cards, now each carrying a small log stamp — 'CONFIRMED: NONEXISTENT', 'CONFIRMED: CONTRADICTS', 'CONFIRMED: OFF-TOPIC'. Beneath, two dimmed captions fade in: 'THREE CHECKED != AIRTIGHT' and 'ONE WRONG != WORTHLESS'.

beats.narration_text: A polished answer is not evidence it's correct. Fluency and accuracy come from different places.

Give me a short checklist for verifying it myself — what to open, what to recompute, and what to trace back to one exact sentence, before I trust any of it. Liam, in for Bear.
